title: Context Engineering, Caching, RAG & Memory
scopeHtml: Scope: staying in the context budget, prompt caching, token counting, RAG vs agentic search, memory scope, Skills, multimodal input and the Message Batches API.

notes.title: Context budget
notes.html:
The core idea. The context window is a fixed budget that holds, at once: the system prompt, the conversation history, injected documents, tool definitions, every tool result accumulated so far, and the model's output. Tool results are appended and stay for the rest of the session. In a single-turn prompt this is invisible; in a multi-step agent running ten or twenty tool calls the window fills fast, and then the agent either compacts (losing detail) or stalls before the task is done.

Context engineering is the discipline of deciding in advance what goes into the window, what comes back out as a summary, and what never enters at all.

The production-vs-development gap (the receipts postmortem). An agent processed sales receipts under a 40k-token budget that the team set as a cost control (the model itself had far more room: current models carry at least 200k tokens, and the newest flagship models serve 1M by default). In development: twenty receipts at ~800 tokens per tool result, ~18k total for a clean twenty-turn session. In production: receipts came with supporting documentation and averaged ~3,200 tokens per call. Eight turns of tool output alone were ~25,600 tokens; with the system prompt, user and assistant messages the running total hit 40k at turn eight. The symptom was wrong tool selections and incomplete analyses starting at turn eight, which looked like a schema problem. The real cause: the system prompt and early instructions were crowded out by tool outputs never pruned after use, so the agent decided on a context that no longer contained its guidance.

What to do.

  • Measure the actual token cost of a tool result against the largest input you can find in your target data before shipping, not against fixtures.
  • If tool selection degrades after a fixed number of turns, check whether the window is filling before debugging schemas.
  • Use count_tokens (same request body as a messages call; no inference) in development to validate assumptions and in production to gate requests that would exceed the window.
  • Prune tool outputs after use, and apply compaction proactively before the cap is reached.
  • Choose memory scope at design time (see the memory notes): accumulated in-context history across sessions can use 40k+ tokens before the first productive turn.

Real life. A suitcase for a trip. Packing for a weekend (test fixtures) works; packing the same way for a month (production data) means the zip will not close and you leave behind the passport.

Tech. A log buffer sized for staging traffic that overflows under production load.

Exam traps. Blaming tool schemas for a context problem; assuming the model's maximum window is your working budget; forgetting that images, PDFs and MCP tool definitions also consume budget.

notes.title: Pruning, compaction, clearing and subagents
notes.html:
Four strategies, each fitting a different conversation shape.

Strategy What it does When What you lose
Pruning (rewind) jump back to an earlier message and continue, removing what came after Claude went down an unproductive path, or debugging back-and-forth won't help the next task the work after the rewind point; Claude must relearn anything useful from it
Compaction (/compact in Claude Code; server-side compaction in the API, a beta strategy; or manual summarization client-side) summarize history into a condensed version preserving key information session nearing the ceiling but you want to continue the same feature anything the summary omitted
Clearing (/clear in Claude Code; a new session in the API) start with empty context next task is completely different; old context would only bias or confuse everything unless persisted (e.g. in CLAUDE.md)
Subagent handoff a subagent works in its own isolated context with only the task description and system prompt it needs, returns a summary self-contained subtasks, especially exploration whose journey would clutter the main context but whose answer is short visibility into how the subagent got there

Compaction quality is the summarizer's prompt. In Claude Code, /compact decides the summary content. With manual compaction in an API session you write the summarizer prompt, and that prompt determines what the agent knows afterwards.

  • "Summarize the conversation so far" → a generic summary that may drop task-critical state (which files were modified, what was decided at a branch point, which error occurred and how it was resolved).
  • "Summarize, preserving all file paths modified, all decisions made, and any errors encountered and their resolutions" → a summary the agent can use. Task-critical state loss from an under-specified summarizer is one of the most common sources of multi-session agent failures.

Subagent handoffs for long-horizon tasks. When a task is too large for one window, a bigger window is not the fix; decompose and pass each subagent only what it needs: a scoped task, the directly relevant results of prior steps, its tools, and clear exit conditions. The parent collects results. This keeps per-turn cost low. It adds implementation overhead, so use it where context cost is a real constraint; a simple single-turn prompt does not need it. Design it at the architecture stage rather than patching it in after the failure.

Choosing. Dead-end exploration → prune. Same task near the ceiling → compact (with a good summarizer). Unrelated task → clear (persist what must survive). Self-contained noisy subtask → subagent.

Real life. Moving house: rewind (undo the last box), compact (vacuum-pack clothes, lose shape), clear (empty flat), subagent (a mover packs the garage and hands you one inventory sheet).

Tech. Git: revert, squash, new branch, and a CI job that reports one status.

notes.title: Prompt caching
notes.html:
The problem it solves. Every request reprocesses its entire input from scratch, including parts identical to the last request, and you pay for that each time. Caching stores the processing work done on a stable prefix so follow-up requests reuse it at a fraction of the cost and latency.

Mechanics.

  • The first request writes the prefix to cache; later requests that send identical content up to the same point read it.
  • Matching is on an exact prefix: a single changed character before the cache point (even adding "please") invalidates the cache and forces a fresh write.
  • You enable it by marking a cache breakpoint with cache_control of type ephemeral on the last block you want cached; everything up to and including that block is cached. There is no global switch. You can place up to four breakpoints. (There is also an automatic mode: a single top-level cache flag where the system manages breakpoints as the conversation grows; recommended as a starting point.)
  • The request is processed in the fixed order tools → system prompt → messages, so a breakpoint after the tools caches the tool definitions while keeping messages dynamic.
  • Content after the last breakpoint is processed normally.

Lifetime. Default 5 minutes, refreshed on each read. Opt-in 1 hour with ttl: "1h" on the breakpoint, useful for agents that pause between steps (a 20-minute gap would otherwise expire the 5-minute cache and you'd pay the write again with no read benefit).

Economics.

  • Cache writes cost a premium over base input: about 1.25x (5-minute TTL) or 2x (1-hour).
  • Cache reads cost a fraction, about 0.1x.
  • So it only pays when reads outnumber writes.

Minimum length. Caching applies only above a minimum token threshold (about 1,024 tokens for most current models); shorter prompts are not cached even with a breakpoint.

Three conditions for a win. (1) Content identical between requests, (2) the same content recurs soon enough (within TTL), (3) the prefix is long enough. Best candidates: a long system prompt, a large tool schema set, a reference document you query repeatedly; ideal for high-volume systems with a long fixed system prompt.

Trade-offs. The cache holds the prefix as of its write, so if the prefix must reflect changing data you accept a consistency window; for fixed prompts and stable tool schemas nothing goes stale. Put volatile content (timestamps, user names) after the last breakpoint.

Combined with batching. For non-urgent jobs that reuse context, the batch discount and caching compound.

Real life. A gym locker: pay once to set up your gear, then every visit is cheap, but only if you come back before the day pass expires and nothing in the locker moved.

Tech. A CDN cache keyed on the exact URL; add a timestamp to the URL and you never get a hit.

notes.title: RAG and agentic search
notes.html:
Why retrieval. A model reads everything in context for every request, so loading all documents up front consumes the window and leaves less room for work. Retrieval-augmented generation stores material outside the window, finds the parts relevant to the current request, and supplies only those at request time. Two properties: it scales (per-request cost stays flat as the source grows) and it is only as good as what it finds (if retrieval misses the document, the model never sees it). Organize sources well: descriptive names ("Q3 refund policy, updated August 2024") surface better than "notes_final_v3.pdf".

Two forms.

Classical RAG Agentic search
Work upfront: chunk the source, convert chunks to embeddings (vectors capturing meaning), store them; at query time embed the question and fetch the chunks with the most similar vectors at query time: the model searches live sources, reads documents on demand, pulls results as the task unfolds; no pre-built index
Analogy a librarian who pre-wrote a summary card for every chapter a researcher who goes and finds the answer when asked
Strengths inspectable (see which chunks were retrieved, test retrieval directly); cheap and fast per query no index to build, store, sync or secure; always reads current files
Costs infrastructure: index to build, keep in sync, secure more tokens and time per query; less inspectable
Fits stable reference corpus, simple lookups changing corpus, multi-step questions

You may already use agentic search without noticing: Claude Code loads only the MCP tools it needs rather than every definition; Claude.ai Projects surfaces only relevant document sections when a knowledge base outgrows the window.

The three places classical RAG breaks.

  1. Chunking. Too small and a chunk lacks surrounding context; too large and it dilutes the match with unrelated text. Sentence- or section-based chunking with a little overlap is a reasonable default; overlap keeps facts that cross a boundary retrievable.
  2. The embedding match. Similarity search retrieves content semantically close, which isn't always the exact term you need; a query for a specific identifier can miss the right chunk when a more semantically similar one outranks it. Hence lexical match alongside semantic.
  3. Assembly into the prompt. Retrieved chunks must reach the model in the structure the prompt expects, otherwise it answers from memory instead of the retrieved text.

Routing between the two. A cheap classification step can send single-fact lookups to fetch-once and multi-part questions to agentic search, spending on iteration only when needed. Defaulting everything to iterative search inflates cost and latency; defaulting everything to a static index gives shallow answers on multi-step questions. If every query has the same shape, skip the router. (Any reported performance gain of agentic search over an index is version-pinned: confirm it at build time.)

Real life. A librarian with pre-written index cards versus a researcher walking the shelves when you ask.

Tech. Elasticsearch-style index versus grepping the live repository.

notes.title: Memory scope
notes.html:
The question. What should the agent know at the start of the next session, and how much does carrying that cost? Getting it wrong has two opposite failures: too much state in-context inflates every API call (the model re-reads the whole conversation each turn and cost scales with session length); too little persistent state strips memory across sessions (anything not written down vanishes when the conversation ends).

Patterns.

Scope What persists Cost Use when What you lose
In-context state in the active conversation, across turns of one session zero retrieval overhead; token cost grows with the conversation short sessions that fit the window and need no cross-restart survival everything at session end
External storage state written to a database, read back at session start or on demand retrieval latency per call + read/write logic to build state must survive sessions, move between users, or be shared across agent instances nothing on persistence; cost is latency and complexity
Summarized memory a condensed prior conversation injected at the start of the next session lower tokens than replaying history long-running conversational agents whose full history would outgrow the budget any detail the summarizer didn't preserve
Stateless nothing no overhead task-execution agents that finish and close; fully independent pipelines all prior context

Decide at design time. The default path (store full history in messages, resend every call) works in a prototype, then token cost grows every turn, latency climbs, and a long session hits the hard limit. The refactor (move state to external storage, inject only what each turn needs) is mechanical — a few hundred lines and a database the team already has — but happens under production pressure with a deadline, so it costs far more than making the call during design.

The session-four postmortem. A support-escalation agent ran 10 to 15 turn sessions in development with in-context memory. In production, state accumulated across shorter sessions; by session four the injected history exceeded 40,000 tokens before the first tool call and, with system prompt and tool schemas, over 45,000 tokens were consumed before any productive turn. Results became incomplete, looking like a tool-selection failure. Fix: external storage with only the relevant subset injected. Lesson: development used one long session, production used many short ones with accumulated state; those are different shapes.

Guidance. Measure expected state size (history + system prompt + tool schemas) against the limit before choosing in-context as the default. Without caching or compaction, long sessions accumulate cost faster than teams expect.

Real life. A doctor who keeps everything in their head (in-context), keeps patient files (external), reads yesterday's handover note (summarized), or sees a walk-in once (stateless).

Tech. Server-side session in memory vs database vs cached summary vs stateless lambda.

notes.title: Skills
notes.html:
What a Skill is. A reusable markdown file that teaches Claude how to handle a specific kind of task once. It lives in a SKILL.md inside an identified directory with two parts: a frontmatter block (name, description) and the instructions below. The description is the matching criterion: Claude reads the name and description of every available Skill, compares them to your request, and loads the full instructions only on a match. Unmatched instructions never enter the context window. Only name + description load at startup, so the context cost is low.

Skills vs the alternatives.

Pattern When it loads Context cost Best for
Skill (SKILL.md) on demand, when the request matches the description low (name+description at startup; body on match) task-specific expertise that shouldn't inflate sessions where it isn't needed: domain output formats, review checklists, workflows for a subset of tasks
CLAUDE.md every session, unconditionally fixed overhead regardless of task always-on standards: coding conventions, output rules, constraints across all tasks
In-context instructions every turn within that session grows with session length; dies with the session short exploratory, single-conversation work

In the Agent SDK, whether filesystem settings (including CLAUDE.md and skills) load is controlled by settingSources (TypeScript) / setting_sources (Python). Do not rely on a default; set it explicitly.

Runtimes (where the same skill file behaves differently).

  • Claude Code: discovered from .claude/skills on the filesystem, loads on a description match or by name; runs in your terminal session, against local files, under the active permission mode and deny rules.
  • Messages API: sent with the request and run inside the code-execution container, not your environment. Requires two beta headers: code-execution-2025-08-25 and skills-2025-10-02 (verify current values; beta headers change toward GA). A skill that assumes local files or tools won't behave the same.
  • Agent SDK: loaded by the agent the SDK runs, only if settingSources includes the filesystem source. The common surprise: a skill works in Claude Code and does nothing under the SDK because settingSources was never set.
  • Managed Agents: attached when defining the agent resource (not at session time); loaded server-side into a sandbox Anthropic provisions; update the agent definition to change skills.

Portability rules.

  1. Write the description as the matching criterion (a vague one fails to load everywhere).
  2. Don't assume a local filesystem or tools inside the skill body.
  3. Subagents do not inherit skills (nor conversation history; they do inherit the parent's permission context). List needed skills in the subagent's configuration.

Real life. A cookbook index: only titles sit on the shelf face, and you open the recipe when you decide to cook it.

Tech. Lazy-loaded modules.

notes.title: Images, PDFs and batches
notes.html:
Image token cost. Claude views images in 28×28 pixel patches; each patch is one visual token, so an image costs ⌈width/28⌉ × ⌈height/28⌉ tokens. A 1,000×1,000 image is 36×36 = ~1,296 tokens; ten high-resolution screenshots can equal a detailed system prompt. Each model has a maximum native resolution (long-edge and visual-token limits that differ by tier and generation); larger images are downscaled first, so apply the formula to the scaled dimensions. Confirm current limits on the vision docs. Design implication: measure the token cost of a typical production image against the context limit before writing ingestion code; the fix for an over-budget pipeline is often a ten-minute resize step.

Ways to send an image.

Method How Overhead Use when
Inline base64 encode bytes into the message block whole payload travels with every request one-off images
URL public URL in the source block; Claude fetches at request time no payload, but the URL must be stable, public and reachable when fetched already hosted at a stable public URL; not for auth-gated or short-expiry signed URLs
Files API upload once, receive a file_id, reference it later one-time upload; later requests carry the ID same image/PDF across requests, large assets, images across many turns

The Files API is beta and not available on Bedrock or Vertex AI; verify availability for your platform.

PDFs. Use a document block (not image). The source can be base64, a URL or a file_id. There is no required name; optional title (readable name) and context (extra metadata). Token cost considerations and Files API reuse apply the same way.

Prompting multimodal inputs. The same techniques apply; images add ambiguity text lacks (overlap, depth, occlusion). A visual prompt should say how to handle it ("If objects overlap, describe each separately and note the overlap").

The Message Batches API. For the same prompt pattern over hundreds or thousands of inputs, synchronous calls burn threads or hit rate limits.

  • One batch call accepts up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever comes first.
  • You submit, get a batch_id, poll for completion, then download results.
  • Lower per-token cost; completion can take up to 24 hours (often much faster); non-deterministic latency.
  • Results return in arbitrary order; match them to inputs with the custom_id on each request.
Use case Pattern Why
User uploads a photo, expects immediate classification synchronous real-time needed
Nightly pipeline classifying 5,000 records Batches latency not a constraint; cost + async
Eval run of a new prompt on 2,000 examples Batches offline
Chatbot reply synchronous user waiting

Combining. Offline pipelines reusing assets and needing structured output fit well: Files API removes re-uploads, Batches absorbs latency, structured outputs keep results machine-readable. Failure modes: reaching for batch in a user-facing flow (passes tests, fails in production), and underestimating context cost of images.

The classic mistake. "Splitting the list into chunks and looping over the synchronous API" is not batching: the API still sees one request per item and you hit the same rate limits. The Batches API is a different submission model, not a smaller batch size.

Real life. Posting 5,000 letters: you hand the post office one sack (batch) rather than walking to the postbox 5,000 times. It's cheaper but not same-day.

Tech. A bulk insert versus a loop of single inserts.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Budget. Window = system + history + docs + tool definitions + every tool result + output. Tool results persist; production results are bigger than fixtures (800 vs 3,200 tokens in the receipts case), so a 40k budget filled at turn 8 and the symptom was bad tool selection. Measure on largest real inputs; count_tokens; prune and compact proactively.

Strategies. Pruning (rewind), compaction (summarize; quality = summarizer prompt: preserve files modified, decisions, errors + resolutions), clearing (new session; persist in CLAUDE.md), subagent handoff (isolated context returns summary; design early; adds overhead).

Caching. cache_control: ephemeral on the last block to cache, up to 4 breakpoints, order tools→system→messages, exact-prefix match, TTL 5 min (refresh on read) or ttl: "1h", min ~1,024 tokens; writes 1.25x/2x, reads ~0.1x; reads must outnumber writes; dynamic content after the breakpoint.

RAG. Classical (upfront index, inspectable, needs infra) vs agentic search (query-time, no index, more tokens, less inspectable). Breaks in chunking, embedding match (add lexical), assembly. Route lookups vs multi-step.

Memory. In-context, external, summarized, stateless; choose at design time; session-four lesson (many short sessions with accumulated state); measure size first.

Skills. SKILL.md name+description load first, body on match; vs CLAUDE.md (always) and in-context (grows). Runtimes: Claude Code (filesystem), Messages API (code-execution container; headers code-execution-2025-08-25, skills-2025-10-02), Agent SDK (settingSources), Managed Agents (agent resource). Subagents don't inherit skills.

Media and batches. Image tokens ⌈w/28⌉×⌈h/28⌉; send via base64/URL/Files API (beta, not on Bedrock/Vertex); PDFs use document. Batches: ≤100,000 requests/256 MB, ≤24 h, cheaper, arbitrary order → custom_id; chunking a sync loop is not batching.

One-liners.

  • "Measure on production-sized data, not fixtures."
  • "A summary keeps only what the summarizer prompt asks it to keep."
  • "Caching rewards stable prefixes and punishes one changed character."
  • "Batch for offline, sync for humans waiting."

questions.contextHtml: A receipts agent ran 20 clean turns in development (about 800 tokens per tool result, ~18k total, under a 40k team budget). In production tool results average 3,200 tokens. From turn 8 the agent picks wrong tools and returns incomplete analyses.
questions.promptHtml:
What is the most likely cause?

  • A. A bug in the tool schemas
  • B. The context budget is filling: accumulated tool outputs crowd out the system prompt and early guidance; the symptom looks like tool-selection failure
  • C. The model got worse in production
  • D. The API rate-limited the agent

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Rewriting tool descriptions without checking token usage.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the token count per turn? Does failure start at a fixed turn?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Prune tool outputs after use; compact before the cap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Context overflow; schema problem; model change.
  4. How I'd verify each: count_tokens on a real production request.
  5. Root cause: B. Fixtures were 4x smaller than production data.
  6. Fix: Measure against the largest production input, prune and compact proactively, push bulky results out of context.
  7. Prevention: Alert on tokens per turn.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raise the cap blindly.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Tool selection degrades after a fixed number of turns. First check? → Whether the window is filling.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: edits schemas.
  • Hire: spots overflow.
  • Strong hire: quantifies tokens, prunes plus compacts, adds monitoring.

questions.promptHtml:
Match the strategy: after a long debugging dead end, you want to jump back to an earlier message and continue, discarding what followed.

  • A. Compaction
  • B. Clearing
  • C. Pruning (rewind)
  • D. Subagent handoff

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: C. Pruning rewinds to an earlier point and removes the conversation after it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Compaction summarizes history (details can be lost). Clearing starts empty (use for an unrelated next task; persist anything needed, e.g. in CLAUDE.md). Subagent handoff runs a self-contained subtask in an isolated context and returns a short summary (you lose visibility into its steps). With manual compaction, the summarizer prompt decides what survives: tell it to preserve modified file paths, decisions, and errors with their resolutions.

questions.promptHtml:
Which request is the best candidate for prompt caching?

  • A. A short 300-token prompt sent once per hour
  • B. A 20k-token system prompt and tool set reused on every request, several times a minute
  • C. A prompt that starts with the current timestamp then a long document
  • D. A prompt whose first sentence changes per user

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Caching needs a long, identical, frequently reused prefix.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The prefix must match exactly (a changed character before the breakpoint invalidates the cache, so C and D fail), exceed the minimum length (~1,024 tokens on most models, so A fails), and be reused within the TTL (5 minutes refreshed on read; opt-in ttl: "1h"). Mark the last block to cache with cache_control: {type: "ephemeral"}; up to four breakpoints; processing order is tools → system → messages. Writes cost 1.25x (5 min) or 2x (1 h); reads cost about 0.1x, so reads must outnumber writes.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting dynamic content (timestamps, user names) before the cached block.
  • Caching content that must reflect live state.

questions.promptHtml:
A product team has a rapidly changing document set and mostly multi-step questions. They are choosing between a pre-built embedding index and agentic search. Which is generally the simpler fit?

  • A. Classical RAG, because indexes never go stale
  • B. Agentic search: no index to build or sync and it reads current files at query time, at the cost of more tokens and time per query
  • C. Neither; load the whole library into context
  • D. Classical RAG with chunks as large as possible

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Changing corpus plus multi-step questions favors agentic search; a stable corpus with simple lookups favors owning an index.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Classical RAG pays upfront (chunk, embed, store, keep in sync, secure) and is inspectable and cheap per query. RAG breaks in three places: chunking (too small loses context, too large dilutes the match; use overlap), the embedding match (semantic similarity can miss an exact identifier, so add lexical search) and assembly into the prompt. A cheap router can send lookups to fetch-once and multi-part questions to agentic search.

questions.promptHtml:
An agent helps the same support engineer on one case across several days. Which memory scope fits best?

  • A. In-context only; the window is big enough
  • B. External storage (database), reading back only the relevant subset at session start
  • C. Stateless
  • D. Reprint the whole history every call

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. State that must survive sessions belongs outside the context window.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: In-context memory costs more with every turn and is wiped at session end; summarized memory loses whatever the summarizer dropped; stateless suits independent jobs. Decide at design time: retrofitting under production pressure is the expensive version. In a postmortem, accumulated history exceeded 40k tokens before the first tool call of session four.

questions.promptHtml:
A team has a long PR-review checklist used for 10% of tasks. Where should it live to avoid inflating every session?

  • A. CLAUDE.md
  • B. In-context instructions pasted each time
  • C. A Skill (SKILL.md): only name and description load at startup, the body loads when a request matches the description
  • D. A rules file with no paths

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: C. Skills load on demand; CLAUDE.md and unscoped rules load every session.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The description is the matching criterion, so write it as one. Runtime differences matter: Claude Code reads skills from the filesystem; the Messages API needs beta headers code-execution-2025-08-25 and skills-2025-10-02 and runs inside the code-execution container; the Agent SDK needs settingSources/setting_sources set explicitly or skills never load; Managed Agents attach skills to the agent resource. Subagents do not inherit skills (they do inherit the parent's permission context), so list needed skills in their config.

questions.promptHtml:
A nightly job classifies 5,000 customer records and an eval run tests 2,000 examples, and a chatbot answers live users. Which API pattern fits each?

  • A. Synchronous for all three
  • B. Message Batches for the nightly job and the eval run; synchronous for the chatbot
  • C. Message Batches for all three
  • D. Streaming for the nightly job

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Batch trades latency (up to 24 h) for lower cost on offline work; a user waiting needs synchronous or streaming.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A batch holds up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB; you get a batch_id, poll, and results return in arbitrary order, so match them with custom_id. Chunking a list and looping synchronously is not batching. For images, token cost is about ⌈w/28⌉ × ⌈h/28⌉ (1000×1000 ≈ 1,296 tokens); send via base64 (one-off), URL (public, stable) or the Files API (file_id, reuse; beta). PDFs use a document block with the same source options.

questions.promptHtml:
How do you check whether a request will fit before sending it, without paying for generation?

  • A. Send it and catch the error
  • B. Call count_tokens with the same body as a messages call
  • C. Count words and multiply by 1.3
  • D. Ask Claude in the prompt

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. count_tokens returns the token count without running inference.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Use it in development against real tool outputs, and in production to gate oversized requests. Word-count heuristics (C) are model-dependent.

questions.promptHtml:
An agent works for 20 turns on test data but degrades by turn 8 in production. Before editing tool schemas, what do you check first?

  • A. The temperature
  • B. Whether accumulated tool outputs are filling the context window
  • C. The API key
  • D. The network latency

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Context overflow often masquerades as bad tool selection.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Measure tool-result tokens on the largest production inputs, then prune, compact or externalize bulky results.

questions.promptHtml:
You implement manual compaction. Which summarizer instruction best protects the agent's ability to continue?

  • A. "Summarize the conversation."
  • B. "Summarize, preserving all file paths modified, decisions made, and errors encountered with their resolutions."
  • C. "Make it as short as possible."
  • D. "Delete everything but the last message."

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. What the summarizer keeps is all the agent will know afterwards.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A generic summary drops task-critical state, a common source of multi-session failures. Server-side compaction (beta) does it for you when configured.

questions.promptHtml:
The next task is completely unrelated to the current session. Which strategy fits?

  • A. Compaction
  • B. Clearing with a new session (persisting anything needed, e.g. in CLAUDE.md)
  • C. Pruning
  • D. Subagent handoff

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Old context would only add bias or confusion.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The cost is that everything is gone, so durable rules belong in a persistent file.

questions.promptHtml:
A codebase exploration produces a lot of intermediate reading but a short answer. Where should it run?

  • A. In the main context
  • B. In a subagent with its own context, returning a summary
  • C. In a cleared session
  • D. In a batch

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The journey would clutter the main context but the answer is short.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The trade-off is lost visibility into how the subagent reached its conclusion. Subagents add overhead, so apply them only where context cost is a real constraint.

questions.promptHtml:
An agent pauses 20 minutes between steps, reusing a 15k-token prefix. Which setting fits?

  • A. The default 5-minute TTL
  • B. An opt-in ttl: "1h" on the breakpoint
  • C. No caching possible
  • D. Four breakpoints at the end

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The 5-minute window would expire before the next request and you would pay the write again.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The 1-hour write costs more (about 2x vs 1.25x), so it only pays if reads follow.

questions.promptHtml:
After adding "please" to the first line of the system prompt, cache hits drop to zero. Why?

  • A. The cache expired
  • B. Caching needs an exact prefix match, so any change before the breakpoint invalidates it
  • C. Breakpoints are limited to one
  • D. The model changed

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. One changed character before the cache point forces a fresh write.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Keep stable content first (tools, system) and put volatile content after the last breakpoint.

questions.promptHtml:
A search for the exact product code "XJ-4471" misses the right chunk, though semantically similar chunks come back. Which fix addresses it?

  • A. Larger chunks
  • B. Add a lexical (exact-term) match alongside the semantic one
  • C. Remove overlap
  • D. Increase temperature

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Embeddings find meaning, not necessarily exact identifiers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: RAG breaks in three places: chunking, the embedding match and assembly into the prompt.

questions.promptHtml:
A skill that works in Claude Code does nothing under the Agent SDK. Most likely cause?

  • A. The skill file is corrupt
  • B. settingSources / setting_sources was never set, so filesystem skills never loaded
  • C. The model does not support skills
  • D. Skills only run in the browser

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Set it explicitly rather than relying on a default.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: On the Messages API skills need beta headers code-execution-2025-08-25 and skills-2025-10-02 and run in the code-execution container, not your environment.

questions.promptHtml:
Approximately how many visual tokens is a 1,000 × 1,000 image?

  • A. 100
  • B. About 1,296 (⌈1000/28⌉ × ⌈1000/28⌉)
  • C. 10,000
  • D. 28

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Each 28×28 patch is one visual token.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Oversized images are downscaled first, so run the formula on the scaled dimensions. Reuse the same image across requests with the Files API (file_id).
